overview: Imagine a river city of pine houses, stone walls, hot sulfur baths and silver coins, where church bells and the call to prayer crossed the Mtkvari air. Arab armies first secured Tbilisi by treaty in the seventh century; from the 730s, caliphs governed eastern Georgia through an emir there. Local emirs later rebelled, survived the terrible burning of 853, made their office hereditary and stamped their own names beside the caliph's. Georgian kings steadily closed in. By the 1080s the emir dynasty was gone and wealthy city elders governed; David IV captured Tbilisi in 1122 and made it the Georgian capital. Markets, crafts, Muslim worship and learning continued under new rule. The atlas is doubly tricky: it shows the id only from 1100 to 1200, and its lone polygon does not even contain modern Tbilisi. Read that shape as a flawed locator, while coins, chronicles, archaeology and careful source limits tell the city's richer story.

periods.title: Treaty and tribute before the emirate
periods.summary: Habib ibn Maslama's forces imposed a peace-and-security agreement on Tbilisi around 654 to 655. It promised protection while levying households, but this early submission was not yet the later, locally based Emirate of Tbilisi.

periods.title: Arab governors, a garrison city and competing faiths
periods.summary: After the campaigns of the 730s, an appointed emir governed from Tbilisi within a larger caliphal province. Arabic administration and minting grew beside older Georgian Christian communities, vividly but polemically witnessed by Abo's eighth-century martyr story.

periods.title: Shuabid power and Ishaq's challenge to Baghdad
periods.summary: The Shuabid house held the emirate as Abbasid reach weakened. Emir Ishaq ibn Ismail expanded local power and resisted the caliph, drawing an enormous punitive expedition led by the Turkic commander Bugha.

periods.title: A burned capital rebuilds after Bugha
periods.summary: Bugha's army captured and executed Ishaq and burned much of Tbilisi in 853. Yet the city and its mint revived: surviving silver dirhams dated 862 to 63 show caliphal Arabic writing and exchange only a decade later.

periods.title: Jaffarid emirs make the office hereditary
periods.summary: From roughly the 880s, the Jaffarid family converted an appointed office into a dynasty. Regional powers still intervened; Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj occupied Tiflis around 900. Even so, local emir rule endured.

periods.title: Named emirs, silver messages and a shrinking territory
periods.summary: Tenth- and early eleventh-century dirhams put local emirs' names beside the caliph's, signaling practical independence while preserving religious legitimacy. Coins recover rulers absent from chronicles, even as Georgian powers compressed the emirate toward Tbilisi.

periods.title: Bagratid pressure, disputed control and Seljuk shock
periods.summary: Bagrat IV entered Tbilisi amid invitations and negotiations, but durable annexation failed. Seljuk campaigns devastated the region in 1068 and rearranged local overlordship; the last Jaffarid decades were politically narrow and contested.

periods.title: City elders govern after the emirs disappear
periods.summary: When the Jaffarid line ended in the 1080s, leading citizens governed collectively, reportedly rotating authority. They sought outside protection as David IV tightened control, and the atlas begins in 1100 during this post-emir civic phase.

periods.title: Georgian capital beneath a lingering atlas label
periods.summary: David IV took Tbilisi in 1122 and made it the Georgian kingdom's capital. Muslim worship, law and scholarship continued under privileges, while the imported emirate polygon lingers until the 1200 seam, seventy-eight years beyond conquest.

sections.title: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon

items.text: The exact indexed id is emirate-of-tiflis, labeled “Emirate of Tiflis” and marked circa 1100 to 1200. Coverage records one border file and no card or completed review. Its imported summary itself says emirs ruled effectively only to about 1080 and the city fell in 1122, so the database dates are map coverage, not a dynasty's lifetime.

At the 1000 snapshot the target id is absent, even though Jaffarid emirs historically still ruled in Tbilisi. The broad imported `georgia` polygon owns every audited eastern Georgian city point. This predecessor seam proves that absence from one atlas layer cannot be read as proof that a polity did not exist.

At 1100 the target appears once as an unlabeled Polygon: one part, one ring and only seven positions. Its bounds are 44.8906° to 45.8339° east and 41.0977° to 41.7087° north; its coordinate-array SHA-256 is `0b1e8ea8b03040ea69734d51090a11e799fe1fc89177811132b93263f53c24b1`. Those are exact digital facts, not reconstructed medieval frontiers.

The strangest result is geographic: the exact modern Tbilisi coordinate lies outside the emirate polygon and inside the separate Georgia polygon. Every named audit point misses the target. Raw topology shows shared boundary arcs only with `georgia` and `kakheti-hereti`. The tiny shape sits southeast of its supposed capital, so it should be treated as displaced imported geometry.

At 1200 the emirate id vanishes and Georgia owns Tbilisi, Mtskheta, Rustavi, Gori, Dmanisi, Telavi and Kutaisi; it remains absent at 1279. Historically, city elders had replaced the emirs by the 1080s and David IV captured city and citadel in 1122. The atlas therefore starts late and ends seventy-eight years after conquest.

sections.title: From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government

items.text: Arab forces first secured Tbilisi by a peace-and-security agreement around 654 to 655. The transmitted terms protected lives and worship while demanding payment by household. Modern scholarship warns that early treaty texts passed through later writers, so the agreement is evidence for submission and taxation, not a perfectly preserved form signed at a medieval desk before us.

The emirate took shape after the great Arab campaigns of the 730s. Its emir was originally a caliph-appointed official subordinate to a provincial governor, not automatically an independent king. From Tbilisi, early administrators claimed wide authority in eastern Georgia, while local nobles, churches and mountain communities continued to exercise power of their own.

A Kufic Arabic inscription from Tiflis dated Sha'ban AH 147, or 764 to 765 CE, and early mint evidence show Arabic as an official written language in the city. That does not mean everyone spoke Arabic at home: inscriptions reveal the language chosen by administrators and moneyers much more clearly than the speech of every Georgian, Armenian or other resident.

Abo's near-contemporary story gives a human-scale window into the eighth-century city. He was a young Arab skilled at mixing myrrh preparations who traveled with the Georgian ruler Nerse, learned among Christians and eventually died for refusing to abandon Christianity. Because the text is a martyr tale, its theology is central and its scenes are not neutral census notes.

Tbilisi sat in a steep Mtkvari valley with a fortress commanding crossings and routes. Government depended on more than a city wall: tribute collectors, soldiers, messengers and negotiations linked the capital to subordinate towns and countryside. Claims of control shrank over time, reminding us that an emir's title and his day-to-day reach were not always identical.

sections.title: Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver

items.text: By the early ninth century the Shuabid emirs were turning an appointment into local family power. Ishaq ibn Ismail became strong enough to challenge Baghdad. Caliph al-Mutawakkil responded with Bugha al-Kabir's 853 expedition, showing the emirate's central puzzle: it belonged to the Abbasid political world yet repeatedly tried to act on its own.

Bugha's forces crossed the Mtkvari, took Tbilisi, burned the city and executed Ishaq. Medieval writers give enormous army and death totals; these are reported figures, not modern demographic measurements. The safest conclusion is still grim: the assault was catastrophic, involved regional allies on both sides and failed to create lasting, tight caliphal control.

Nine or ten years after the burning, Tbilisi was striking Abbasid silver again. Six known dirhams dated AH 248, or 862 to 63, name the mint and caliph al-Musta'in. A coin cannot tell us how every street recovered, but minting requires skilled dies, metal, standards and officials. That is small, round evidence that urban institutions had resumed.

From about the 880s the Jaffarids made emir rule hereditary for roughly two centuries. Coin sequences identify Mansur ibn Ja'far, Ja'far ibn Mansur and Ali ibn Ja'far, some barely visible in narrative sources. Numismatics supplies names and dates, while gaps and disputed readings warn against pretending we own a complete ruler-by-ruler diary.

A dirham of Ja'far ibn Mansur dated AH 374, or 984 to 85, adds one exact point to the dynasty's story. Later issues carried a local emir's name beside the caliph's, expressing political independence without discarding the caliph's religious prestige. Medieval money was payment, official announcement and pocket-sized family tree all at once.

sections.title: Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel

items.text: The emirate never lived alone inside a neat border. Around 900, Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj campaigned across Armenia and Caucasian Albania and occupied Tiflis after fighting King Smbat. His intervention connects the city to caliphal appointments, Azerbaijan and Armenian politics; it did not erase the longer Jaffarid line that resumed local rule.

By the eleventh century the united Georgian monarchy pressed hard around Tbilisi. Bagrat IV entered its citadel in 1045 after city elders invited him, yet shifting factions and negotiations prevented a simple permanent takeover. Medieval allegiance could change through invitation, hostage-taking, siege, tribute or bargain, not only through one decisive flag-raising moment.

Seljuk expansion changed the balance again. Alp Arslan and allies devastated Tbilisi and Kartli in 1068 and assigned Tbilisi and Rustavi to the ruler of Ganja; Bagrat then fought and arranged tribute with local heirs. These rapid switches explain why one colored polygon cannot capture overlordship, city government and military occupation simultaneously.

After the Jaffarid line ended in the 1080s, Tbilisi's ‘elders’ became full rulers. The Academy entry describes them as representatives chosen from wealthy citizens; al-Fariqi says leading people rotated authority month by month. That sounds almost like a city council, but it represented an upper urban group rather than every craft worker, widow or child.

Tbilisi, Dmanisi and Ganja appealed for outside help as David IV's campaigns tightened around them. A Muslim coalition met his army at Didgori in 1121 and lost; the following year David secured Tbilisi. The Academy source is clear about the strategic sequence, while spectacular medieval army totals remain too disputed for this children's card.

sections.title: A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops

items.text: Arabic geographers describe Tbilisi on both banks of the Mtkvari, defended by walls and gates and connected across the river. Roads led toward Armenia, Iran, the Caspian and mountain passes. A merchant's day depended on bridges, pack animals, interpreters, tolls and safety; ‘crossroads’ meant hard logistical work, not goods magically sliding along a map line.

Geographers praise fertile surroundings, fruit and crops and list honey, wool, felt and silk textiles among products or traded goods. Such lists show availability and commercial reputation, not what every poor household owned. Silk could be an expensive bolt in a merchant's store while a felt item or wool cloth served a very different budget.

The mint linked politics to market life. The AH 248 dirham was silver, roughly 26 millimetres across in listed specimens, and carried long formulas around a tiny field. Moneyers had to fit legible script onto metal smaller than many cookies, an accurate bit of medieval design pressure, with no need to imagine coins as modern pocket change.

Ninth- through thirteenth-century eastern Georgian workshops made red- and light-clay bowls and dishes with slips, colored glazes and plant, animal or human motifs. Finds include a medieval Tbilisi pottery workshop. The date range crosses 1122, so these objects document urban craft continuity, not a perfectly labeled ‘emirate-only’ cupboard.

Dmanisi, once tied to the emirate's wider urban network, preserves houses, storerooms, workshops, glass and pottery production, walls, a bath and a long water-access tunnel. It helps show what a regional city could require, but it lies about eighty kilometres away and many remains are later; it cannot become a substitute floor plan for Tbilisi.

sections.title: Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city

items.text: Muslims governed the city, but Christians remained visible. Written sources imagine a soundscape where Islamic prayer and Christian worship occupied the same city. Coexistence did not mean modern equality or never fighting; Abo's execution and the earlier protection agreement show both pressure and negotiated space.

A congregational mosque, its preacher or khatib, and a qadi who judged Muslim cases were key institutions. In 1122 a khatib and qadi reportedly negotiated for the city. Later rebuilding makes the exact emirate-era mosque difficult to identify archaeologically, so the card names documented offices without drawing an invented perfect building.

Christian writing did not vanish under Muslim rulers. Ioane Sabanisdze composed Abo's martyrdom in Georgian near the event, framing the city through scripture and resistance. It proves skilled Georgian literary production and a Christian audience; because hagiography aims to inspire belief, its speeches and wonders demand a different reading from a tax record or coin.

Dmanisi's medieval cemetery contains Georgian, Armenian and Arabic inscriptions and Muslim and Christian sectors. That multi-confessional record belongs to another emirate-linked city and extends beyond 1122, yet it provides material evidence that people of several languages and religions lived, died and remembered relatives in the same regional urban world.

Biographical sources connect Tbilisi with Sunni, Shi'i and later Sufi scholars, but Djaparidze stresses how scant the evidence is: no local Muslim city chronicle survived, and distant biographers favored people who became famous elsewhere. Religious variety is supported; precise percentages, neighborhood maps and a year-by-year conversion graph are not.

sections.title: Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record

items.text: The seventh-century agreement assessed a levy per household, so families were units through which government counted responsibility. It never supplies a standard household size or says every home contained the same relatives. A ‘family’ might include several generations, dependents or workers, but those possibilities must remain questions rather than manufactured statistics.

At the social top stood emirs, military commanders, landholding nobles and wealthy citizens; after the 1080s the elders represented the upper urban layer. Below that record-rich ceiling were merchants, craftspeople, servants, carriers and agricultural workers. Surviving texts name officeholders far more readily than the people hauling water, sweeping shops or tending ovens.

The al-Tiflisi biographies include jurists, poets, physicians, merchants, craftspeople and statesmen. A name ending in al-Tiflisi signals association with Tbilisi, not automatically ethnicity, birthplace or lifelong residence. This caution matters in a mixed city: scholars cannot turn every bearer into an Arab settler, converted Georgian or permanent resident without more evidence.

Broader Georgian legal evidence places dowry and some women's property interests as early as the ninth century, but emirate-specific documents rarely name ordinary women. That regional evidence suggests women participated in household property; it cannot establish equal inheritance, a typical dowry or the daily authority of a Tbilisi mother, widow or craftswoman.

Abo was about seventeen or eighteen when he reached this world and was already skilled at mixing fragrant or medicinal substances. His case shows a young person could learn a specialized craft and languages, but it is one exceptional hagiographic life. It does not give a normal school age, apprenticeship contract or chores chart for Tbilisi children.

sections.title: Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin

items.text: Djaparidze found fifty-two people bearing the al-Tiflisi nisba in eighth- through fourteenth-century Arabic and Persian sources. Some traveled to Baghdad, Damascus and other study centers; several stayed abroad. This reveals a far-reaching learning network while also showing why fame overseas can distort our view of who taught children inside Tbilisi itself.

Al-Hasan ibn Bundar al-Tiflisi studied Arabic poetry and grammar around the tenth and early eleventh centuries and dedicated a work to Emir Ali ibn Ja'far. His lost books show a learned circle connected to the court. Loss matters: a title and later biography cannot reconstruct a classroom, library shelves or what his pupils, if any, actually read.

The physician and Syriac-to-Arabic translator Isa al-Raqqi al-Tiflisi served Sayf al-Dawla's court in Aleppo. A later Tiflis-born scholar, Hubaysh, wrote on medicine and astronomy after migrating west. Both lives demonstrate intellectual mobility, not a documented city hospital back home; court biographies reveal fame far better than ordinary healthcare access.

Christian learning in eleventh- and twelfth-century Georgia centered strongly on churches and monasteries, while advanced students sometimes traveled abroad and new academies emerged around David IV's age. This is regional context, not evidence that every Tbilisi child attended class. Most practical learning likely happened through households and work, though attendance figures do not survive.

Written-language sample, official Arabic mint legend, Tbilisi, AH 248 / 862 to 63: `بسم الله ضرب هذا الدرهم بتفليس سنة ثمان و اربعين و مائتين`. Transliteration: `bismi llāh ḍuriba hādhā al-dirham bi-Tiflīs sanat thamān wa-arbaʿīn wa-miʾatayn`. Translation: “In the name of God, this dirham was struck at Tbilisi in the year 248.” This is formal coin Arabic, not everyday conversation.

sections.title: Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play

items.text: An Arabic source remarked that Tbilisi houses were built largely of pine, while walls and fortress works used more durable materials. Timber burns and rots, so surviving stone exaggerates elite and defensive architecture. We can picture a wooden city around its citadel, but no checked source supplies a universal room count, roof plan or furniture set.

Wool, felt and silk textiles appear in geographic descriptions of Tbilisi's products and trade. They prove textile work and exchange, not one citywide costume. Wealth, occupation, faith, season and origin all affected dress; the responsible card cannot put every child into a silk robe simply because silk passed through the market.

The city's fertile surroundings supplied crops and fruit, and geographers mention honey and watermills. Those clues support bread or grain foods, fruit and sweetening within the food system, but they do not preserve a weekly menu or portion sizes. Modern dishes are not pushed backward nine centuries merely because they taste wonderfully Georgian today.

Excavations in medieval Tbilisi found kilns and many vessel forms, including bowls, jugs, pots, oil lamps, salt holders, inkpots and lids, along with defective workshop pieces. Some layers are twelfth to thirteenth century or later, so they illuminate continuity across conquest. A cracked bowl in a waste pit is still evidence of making, using and discarding things.

No checked emirate-specific source preserves children's game rules, toys securely dated to this polity or a street-song melody. Bells, calls to prayer and recited sacred texts certainly made sound, and decorated bowls could delight the eye. Yet a coin can reveal an emir's name much more readily than whether children played tag after chores.

sections.title: Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap

items.text: Abo's skill mixing myrrh preparations and Isa al-Tiflisi's later fame as physician and translator show specialized knowledge of substances and healing. Neither source describes a public Tbilisi clinic, childbirth routine or care available to poor families. One craft-trained youth plus one migrant court doctor cannot become a complete healthcare system by wishful arithmetic.

The eleventh-century Georgian Ustsoro Karabadini is a medical handbook drawing on regional and classical traditions and discussing remedies, including medicinal uses of wine. It proves written medicine in the broader Georgian world during the emirate's later centuries. It does not prove that a Tbilisi practitioner owned this exact book or followed every recipe.

Tbilisi's naturally hot sulfur water made baths famous to medieval geographers; hot water did not need a wood fire before entering the bathing system. Baths offered washing and social space, but the checked sources do not give an emirate-era timetable, price list, gender schedule or exact number. Even naturally hot plumbing leaves cold historical questions.

Water could come from the Mtkvari, wells and ceramic pipes from nearby ravines. A modern study traces that long tradition but explicitly says exposed pipe lines cannot be securely dated without more archaeology. Fetching and carrying water therefore remained crucial work; which house had direct supply in 900 is not something the evidence settles.

The archaeological report identifies reservoirs and clay tubes and says broken pottery was sometimes buried or thrown into the Mtkvari. It does not securely identify an emirate-period household toilet, latrine network, sewer or wiping material. We know where some smashed pots went; the hoped-for medieval bathroom tour remains stubbornly unavailable.

ending.text: David IV captured Tbilisi and its citadel in 1122, ending the post-Jaffarid elders' sovereignty and absorbing the city into the Kingdom of Georgia. Tbilisi became the Georgian capital, while Muslim residents retained worship, legal and scholarly institutions under negotiated privileges. The atlas endpoint of 1200 is a delayed geometry handoff, seventy-eight years after conquest.
